utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-5/18-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and Iain Reid appearing for the Prosecution -- excuse me, and Ann Sutherland. I got into a litany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you are following these proceedings in the language you understand, and I also take it that you are appearing on your own today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, you are right on both counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Pre-Trial Conference held pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Tribunal's Rules in order to make the final arrangement for the commencement of the trial. For this reason, we are sitting as a Bench comprised of myself, Judge Howard Morrison, Judge Melville Baird, and Judge Flavia Lattanzi as our Reserve Judge. However, since Judge Baird has decided to refrain from sitting pending the accused's motion to disqualify him, we are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis. The Chamber had previously decided that the trial would commence on Monday, 19th of October, 2009, following which Mr. Karadzic filed an application for a certification to appeal, which we granted. The Appeals Chamber is currently considering the matter and will render its decision in due course. Should the Appeals Chamber not issue its decision before 14th of October, the Trial Chamber will need to consider staying the commencement of trial until such time as the Appeals Chamber's decision is issued. However, until that time, we must continue to work on the basis that the trial will commence as planned. I wish to inform you, however, that for administrative reasons the Trial Chamber intends to commence the trial on Wednesday, 21st of October, rather than the 19th, and will sit that week for two days, being 21st and 22nd October, in the mornings. Before turning to some of the procedural issues associated with the commencement of the trial, I will first deliver on behalf of the Chamber our decision on the application of Rule 73 bis. On 22nd July 2009, the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to make written submissions on how Rule 73 bis (D) may be utilised to reduce the size of the trial and ensure that it is conducted fairly and expeditiously. The Prosecution filed its submission on 31st of August, making a number of proposals. First, it reduced the length of time required for the examination-in-chief of its proposed viva voce and Rule 92 ter witnesses by moving a number of witnesses to a reserve list and re-assessing the time required for each of the remaining witnesses. It also proposed the reduction of a number of crime sites or incidents alleged in the indictment, removing several municipalities in their entirety from the scope of the trial, as well as several specific crime sites or incidents within the remaining municipalities. Following a discussion on the matter at the Status Conference held on 8th of September, 2009, the Prosecution made a second written submission on 18th September, stating that it could not reduce the municipalities or crime sites and incidents any further without doing damage to its case as a whole, but further revising the time needed for the presentation of its evidence in chief down to 252 hours. The accused filed a written response on 30th of September, without making any specific proposals or submissions in relation to the matter. The Trial Chamber has carefully considered how to exercise its Rule 73 bis powers, in light of the parties' submissions and the observations made at the 8th of September Status Conference concerning the length of the trial as a whole and the practical realities that the Chamber and the parties must face. It emphasises again that its paramount interest is ensuring a trial that is conducted fairly, including fairness to the accused and to the Prosecution and the victims that the Prosecution represents, as well as expeditiously so that justice is done. First, the Chamber appreciates the efforts made by the Prosecution in its first written submission to reduce the crime sites and incidents that will be the subject of this trial. The Chamber accepts each of the proposals for reduction made by the Prosecution and determines pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D) that the Prosecution may not present evidence in respect of the crime sites and incidents identified by it. Despite the efforts of the Chamber to encourage the Prosecution to identify further crime sites and incidents that might be omitted from the scope of this trial, the Prosecution has disappointingly chosen not to do so. The Chamber remains gravely concerned about the scope of the Prosecution's case; however, without yet having a detailed understanding of the Prosecution's case or evidence and in the absence of assistance from the Prosecution, it is extremely difficult for the Chamber to select additional crime sites or incidents for removal. Therefore, the Chamber has decided to adopt another approach. In addition to the reductions suggested by the Prosecution's first written submission, the Chamber will exercise its power under Rule 73 bis (C) to determine the time available to the Prosecution for the presentation of its evidence. In light of the various proposals made by the Prosecution and the Chamber's own time calculations, we consider that Prosecution should lead all of its evidence within a total of 300 hours. This figure is to include its examination-in-chief and any re-examination of its viva voce and Rule 92 ter witnesses, including any witnesses whose evidence is denied admission under Rule 92 bis. It also includes time for any witnesses who have been placed on the Prosecution's reserve witnesses list and who the Prosecution determines during the course of its case in chief that it needs to call. Given that this figure of 300 hours is close to the amount of time which would be allowed to the Prosecution to present its case, if the Prosecution case is to last for a year with the Chamber sitting five days a week, and that the Prosecution has been allowed much more time than the final version of its estimate of time for the presentation of its case which was 252 hours and even the Prosecution's original estimate before any reductions of crime sites and incidents was less than this number, i.e., 293 hours, the Prosecution should be able to finish its case within this time-limit and should not exceed it in any event. In the interest of clarity, the Prosecution should file a marked-up version of the indictment and its schedules based upon appendix B to its 31st August submission and this decision with each of the municipalities and/or crime sites or incidents that will be -- that will not be the subject of evidence at trial struck through. Where the crime site or incident that has been thus removed is not the subject of specific schedule or is subsumed within a scheduled site or incident that remains part of the trial, the Prosecution should use footnotes to explain those charges that have been removed and those that remain part of the trial so that the accused can understand what charges are remaining clearly. This marked-up version of the indictment should be filed publicly by 19th of October, 2009. This is the Chamber's decision which will be followed shortly by a written version. Having dealt with this now I come to the procedural guide-lines issue. Shortly after this Pre-Trial Conference, the Chamber is minded to issue an order setting out certain procedural guide-lines for the conduct of this trial. We have already carefully considered the written submissions of the parties on this matter, and I wish to raise a few items for discussion before we finalise our order. First, with respect to opening statements, both the Prosecution and the accused wish to make opening statements at the commencement of the trial. The accused has requested time equal to that of the Prosecution for his opening statement, but the Prosecution has not indicated how much time it envisages taking. I would like, therefore, to ask Mr. Tieger how much time it will take for your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know if the Court has had an opportunity to look at the times allotted in related or comparable cases, but we did take a look at that and that assessment as we saw it was actually confirmed by the materials prepared today for opening. So the Prosecution would ask the Court to allot two days for the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if the trial is to be commencing on 21st of October, you will need that whole week, given that we are sitting for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a different way of looking at it, but I guess it comes down to that, Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you'll -- you would then request for two days as well for your opening statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. I would really require the same amount of time. If I'm able to present my case earlier, I can finish earlier. But now this is a good opportunity to reiterate that this commencement date goes beyond any reasonable possibility for me to be prepared regarding my submission and appeal, but I'm going to use the time that is going to be allocated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, on your part do you have any observation as to the opening statement by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, nothing comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next issue that I have on my agenda is the modalities of the conduct of the trial, in particular on the part of the accused in terms of his self-representation. Mr. Karadzic has requested that during the course of the trial the Chamber grant right of audience to his legal advisor, Mr. Peter Robinson, so that he can intervene on legal matters on behalf of the accused. He has also asked that his assigned case managers and another of his assigned legal associates be permitted access to the courtroom without rights of audience to assist him in the conduct of his defence. Before deciding this matter, I would like to hear from you, Mr. Karadzic, on precisely the role you envisage for Mr. Robinson in the proceedings. What kinds of legal issues do you intend for him to speak on, or can you give us examples of other types of scenarios where you would wish him to be actively engaged in arguments or submissions. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, what I envisage as a role of Mr. Robinson would be something that I, myself, would have to allocate as the time for consultations on exclusively legal issues that have nothing to do with the factual situation; in other words, that would be an attempt on my part for -- to gain and offset the time that we might use for preparation in order to ensure a smooth conduction of proceedings. Therefore, I will have an opportunity not to waste any time when it comes to legal issues. These are procedural matters, solely procedural matters, whereas as for the factual issues, I shall be solely responsible to conduct my case and Mr. Robinson would only have an advisory role, and by my authority he would point to -- we possibly would object in terms of procedural matters. So in my view, that would be exclusively advantageous for a smooth and expeditious conduct of the trial, and I reckon that this is a concession on my part and a contribution as well for these proceedings to be administered without any hindrance that might possibly arise from my need to consult my associates, just like the other party in the proceedings is doing, meaning consulting in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you imagine that he would have any part in the cross-examination of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Excellency. I'm going to lead my defence case by myself in its entirety. But instead of asking for a break, an adjournment, to consult with my associates, my associates will be here on the spot, just like the other party have their associates available at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your submission, Mr. Karadzic, regarding the remuneration of the legal advisor, you compared the role to be played by Mr. Robinson to that of amicus curiae. However, while the amicus curiae will usually be acting in the interest of justice as a whole, Mr. Robinson will be acting, as you stated, "on behalf of Dr. Karadzic" pursuant to instructions from you. Do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is also -- will be for the benefit of justice, but primarily for the sake of an expeditious trial. I will not waiver any of my rights that I'm entitled in terms of self-representation, but I believe that the presence of my associates here would be beneficial for the expeditious proceedings. As for everything else, it will remain in my hands, and I believe and I'm sure that this is going to be to everyone's satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you envisage is this, that you will have the overall control of your case and you will conduct the examination of witnesses; however, as far as legal matters are concerned, Mr. Robinson will, upon your delegation, represent you. Am I correct in so understanding, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will not be any kind of representation. This is going to amount to assistance. Instead of me putting forward an objection and having consultants outside of the courtroom, Mr. Robinson, with my consent and my instructions, will just point out to what we object with relation to the procedure. So this will not be representation. I will represent myself. Instead of Mr. Robinson sitting outside of the courtroom and providing assistance to me, he will be present with me and thus contribute to a smooth conduct of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in your submission you stated that -- I'll -- I quote: "Dr. Karadzic hereby moves that his legal advisor, Peter Robinson, be given right of audience at the trial to address the Trial Chamber on legal issues on Dr. Karadzic's behalf." So in substance, irrespective of any nomenclatural or semantic discussion, Mr. Robinson will be partially representing you as far as legal matters are concerned. Could you elaborate on this matter again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be no question of representations. I am representing myself fully. But in order to have a smooth and unhindered proceedings, Mr. Robinson will be here on the spot in the courtroom instead of sitting outside of the courtroom. Whatever his advice he can give me, I can verbalise and present myself; but I think it would be better for him to do it himself. The same procedure is applied when it comes to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you are saying at the end of the day is a kind of division of work while you have the overall control?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you talked of Mr. Robinson dealing with procedural matters. I assume by that you don't just mean procedural law, but also issues of substantive law that may fall to be determined during the course of the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that these kind of situations will arise in which Mr. Robinson will consult with me what it is in procedural terms unacceptable for us. As for all other substantive matters, it is I who will be the ultimate decision-maker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Law falls into two quite separate categories. There are those aspects of the law which are known as procedural law, how the case progresses, the rules of the admission of evidence, and things like that; but there is also substantive law, case law which has been determined in other cases, and opinions as to the application of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. I'm assuming that there will be occasions when Mr. Robinson will be, upon your instructions, asked to address the Trial Chamber upon matters of substantive law as well as purely procedural matters. Do you follow the distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to trace this, Your Excellency, but this is how things are. In order for the Trial Chamber to understand this better, let's put it this way. After consulting with Mr. Robinson, I'm going to articulate certain submissions; but if it be more expeditious and if this can facilitate matters, then Mr. Robinson will speak instead of me. If there is any confusion, it will be me who will address the Trial Chamber, but that will require more time for me to consult him here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any -- Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed. The Prosecution has of course also considered this request by Dr. Karadzic, and the Prosecution does not oppose the presence of members of the Defence team in the courtroom. We think, actually, it would be helpful if he gets this assistance. However, we oppose the right of audience that is requested for Mr. Robinson. In the first place, Karadzic's request is incompatible with his continued wish to represent himself fully. In the second phase, granting his request would hinder the efficient and expeditious conduct of the proceedings. Making courtroom submissions - and this is my understanding now even after this discussion - making courtroom decisions [sic] is what is intended, and making such submissions on legal issues is counsel's duty and it's not associates' duty. Except for tasks which he cannot complete because he is detained or in -- otherwise hindered in his work, that's what the associate is meant for, but not making submissions to the Court. The appointment of counsel to a self-represented accused is a limitation to self-representation and, rather, it cannot be complementary to it. So we cannot have an associate acting basically as a counsel and at the same time an accused saying, I do not relinquish any of my right to represent myself. And therefore, we are opposed of this. Giving Peter Robinson the right of audience to make legal submissions in court while Karadzic continues to be fully in charge would hinder the trial process in two ways. First of all, to me, it's even -- now that I heard more on this issue, to me it's still not clear who would do objections, for instance, to questions asked during the examination-in-chief or during the cross-examination because these are basically mixed issues, legally and substantive. So there are also a lot of other issues that are mixed that combine legal elements and also substantive factual -- factual elements. Therefore, I think letting them both talk would lead to confusion. It could even lead to contradictions, and, therefore, I think it should not happen. It would lead to delays, definitely. Tribunal practice has recognised partial self-representation and has actually allowed associates to address the Court. That was, for instance, in the Krajisnik case, an issue on the appeals stage. However, the -- these associates acting as counsel in this part -- in this case was addressing a very discrete legal issue. That's completely different from what Mr. Karadzic has in mind. He wants Robinson to address the Court on all sorts of legal issues, and this is what we cannot agree on, and that's something that actually has so far not been allowed in this courtroom. The Trial Chamber in this case has previously held that the solution to Karadzic's concern that he may need to be relieved from making submissions in court on legal issues, that can be addressed by being represented by counsel. That is what the Trial Chamber actually has found in its decision of the 28th of January, 2009, in its decision on accused's motion for adequate facilities and equality of arms. What -- if the accused wants to be advised on legal issues and if he thinks he is not experienced enough to address the Court on legal and factual issues, then he should actually select a -- to be represented by counsel all through this trial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all I can see here is certain fear with respect to the combination of Mr. Robinson and myself, and that flatters me. That means that I have a good associate. It is a fact, though, that the other side also has several people on their team speaking to the Court, not just the chief Prosecutor or the Prosecutor in charge of this case. At any rate, I can verbalise, I can articulate the advice I receive from Mr. Robinson in this courtroom, but it will certainly lead to a much greater waste of time. One thing is certain, though, I am in charge of the Defence case, and I will never relinquish that role to anybody else. However, I do believe it will be easier for the Chamber if Mr. Robinson were to verbalise, articulate, what he would normally say to me, and it will be less precise and less clear if I were to articulate that. I think it will be harder for the Prosecution, but there will be a greater legal benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave the matter at that. We'll consider the issue and we'll issue our decision, in a decision which will be followed immediately after this Pre-Trial Conference in due course. And then we'll deal with the modalities of examination of Rule 92 ter witnesses. The Trial Chamber is considering an appropriate procedure to put in place with regard to Rule 92 ter or partial Rule 92 ter witnesses. The Chamber is concerned to ensure the use of Rule 92 ter in this case will assist in an expeditious trial while at the same time not resulting in a case record that is unreasonably burdened with repetitious or irrelevant evidence and not prejudicing the rights of the accused. Therefore, the Chamber is contemplating requiring the parties to provide one amalgamated, or consolidated, witness statement for those witnesses who are brought pursuant to Rule 92 ter and who have two or more witness statements or transcripts from previous proceedings. This would not be a new statement, but rather a consolidation, removing repetitious and irrelevant portions of statements and/or transcripts that already exist and have been disclosed. It is Chamber's expectation that the amalgamated statement would be shown to the witness by the calling party well in advance of his or her coming to the courtroom to testify. Any corrections to the amalgamated statement that result from it being shown to the witness shall be incorporated into the statement itself. The final amalgamated statement would be provided to the opposing party and the Chamber at least 48 hours prior to the testimony of the witness. This would also dispense with the need for the supplemental information sheet proposed by the Prosecution in order to correct or add to previously given statements. Before the Chamber issues its order on procedure, I'd like to hear from the parties on this suggestion which I believe has been implemented in at least one other Chamber here at the Tribunal. Prosecution, Mr. Tieger or Ms. -- yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, to me it is not entirely clear what you understand to be an amalgamated statement. What we actually intended to do and actually have already prepared, we have prepared motions or notices, depending on what you prefer to have, with charts addressing the parts of the previous testimonies that we have, specifying the pages that we wanted to have -- wanted to tender, and at the same time also list the associated exhibits. If you consider to be an amalgamated statement to just put us now these references into a text and have the whole -- all these parts that we pick from previous testimonies, if you want this to be the amalgamated statement, that would be easy for us to do and we can also show it to the witness. But if you want us to create an entirely new text -- rather, a summary of an existent testimony, that would be definitely very time-consuming, and I wonder whether we could do that at least for the first ten witnesses. That would be probably quite an issue, a logistic issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In cases where there are more than two, practically several, witness statements including this transcript or previous testimony, Chamber is wondering what point there would be in admitting all of those voluminous statements and transcripts. So what Chamber has in mind is just admitting one consolidated new statement, not admitting the remaining, original, existing previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just in addition to this, we have actually aimed to only always pick one testimony, not several testimonies. So we actually take the same approach like we did in the Rule 92 quater motions, that we just pick one of the previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this guide-line would apply to the case where the Prosecution is minded to produce more than two statements. So as a general rule it would not be applied to the case when the Prosecution is minded to produce only one statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now that that's workable, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any say in relation to this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. The Prosecution can opt for only one statement, but the Defence needs to review all of the statements of that witness. So this isn't much of a help for us. That's one matter. The other matter is that we generally object to all abbreviations of testimony. The best case would be if everybody were to testify viva voce, and in that case we could cross-examine and we would have a completely transparent proceedings. When it comes to 92 ter, I would kindly ask that packages for each witness be delivered prior to the beginning of proceedings so that I can see what do they have against me, what arguments they have against me. Ten days prior or any other abbreviation of the dead-line means that I'm unable to prepare myself adequately, to conduct research out in the field, to have my associates conduct research, which means that prior to the beginning of the trial, I need to be made aware of everything that the Prosecution is minded to present in their case against me. So this is my general comment, general objection, namely, that all the packages of documents, everything pertaining to 92 ter needs to be sent to me in a timely fashion, both when it comes to the accompanying material and the order of witnesses. I think that after 14 years the Prosecution needs to be ready for this case, and there is no reason why the Prosecution should know more than the Defence or the Chamber. All of us need to know identical facts in order to be able to carry out our work properly. If I may also say this, 92 ter should not be applied in case of important witnesses who will testify about significant events which took place on the ground, that's one issue. The other issue is that the Chamber should order the Prosecution that in a public session, verbally they need to read out the entire statement of the witness once the witness confirms it. This needs to be done in a public session. They need to disclose publicly everything that is relevant and important within the material that they're tendering into the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with case-by-case whether specific -- evidence of specific witnesses should be led entirely per 92 ter or partially 92 ter when it arises. As to the disclosure issue, it is true that you have to be disclosed every material, every statement, previous statement, but it will be interest of yourself and to your benefit if you were to receive one consolidated statement, in the sense that you can concentrate on those issues. And it will be much easier for you to notice what the Prosecution is going to lead from this witness. And the time-limit for the disclosure, although I said to the Prosecution at least prior to the 48 hours prior to the testimony, as I noted, they should do so well in advance. It is highly recommended for the Prosecution to disclose the 92 ter packages in a timely manner, as Mr. Karadzic suggested. And the Chamber is also preparing its order regarding the procedural guide-lines to requiring the calling party to read out in court a summary of the witness's evidence. It will be reflected in its order to be followed. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just make at least one and perhaps two observations, primarily dealing with the logistics. I think it's clear what the Court has in mind by way of the consolidation and the primary purpose behind that. It does occur to me, however, that there will be occasions where the intent and advantage gained in so doing will be offset by certain logistical issues. I think -- that presumes, I would assume, that the -- that Word versions of the relevant documents are available so they can be -- it can be a cut-and-paste. I'm confident the Court doesn't have in mind that in the hectic pace of trial that someone would be designated to actually re-type or re-form those documents. So it does occur to me that there are circumstances where that is the case. I did a quick check by e-mail and with Mr. Reid as to whether there are circumstances like that. I would certainly ask that in those circumstances that the intent of consolidating, to make it an easier process for everyone to have it at their finger-tips, give way to the reality of the situation and that there's some form of identifying in perhaps two statements, sometimes perhaps three, the relevant portions and consolidating them in a more mechanical way, rather than in one document that has been painstakingly reconfigured. So I'm essentially asking for a pragmatic approach as we try to move forward in a way that makes it easier for the Bench and for the parties to identify the material that will be led and to work with that material. So where we can do so effectively and efficiently and without undue cost, we're certainly prepared to. But where it invites an additional burden that I don't think anyone really intends, we would ask for more flexible application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Setting aside -- apart from setting a general rule, the Chamber can without doubt deal with the specific cases on a case-by-case basis to address the specific needs arising at the time. I've -- however, Mr. Tieger, do you envisage that this situation where you have to produce a consolidated or amalgamated statement would start only when the witness comes to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand there has been -- let me -- and it occurs to me that this matter may involve more complexities than a pure at first blush. So I'm glad the Court is inquiring about this. I understand the Court's concerns in the past about the proofing of witnesses immediately before they testify and occasions on which those have given rise to new information of such a nature that the proceedings have been delayed or the cross-examination needs to be delayed, and so on. It's certainly our intention to meet with our witnesses as early as we can for all purposes, including proofing or the identification of 92 ter packages. However, looking back on previous trials and the conduct of those trials and the availability of counsel to meet with those witnesses and the length of statements involved, including statements given previously under oath or signed statements that had previously been given, I think it must be clear that it would be logistically impossible to devise a system that calls upon the Prosecution or the Defence at any point to essentially re-create the same process that was painstakingly undergone before and that gave rise to those very statements. So by virtue of the process envisaged by 92 ter, the submission of previous testimony given under oath and clearly the identification of the most relevant parts of those testimonies, the -- the -- any procedure that would require the Prosecution essentially to re-do that entire process with the witness before submission of the 92 ter package I think would be logistically impossible, and further I don't think it would advance the interest of the proceedings in any event. So I am giving you the benefit of our reactions to the proposal or the suggestions made by the Court as we think them through, but I am concerned about unforeseen or not fully considered consequences of this. And that's the first one that comes to mind. I suspect that on 30-minutes' reflection, there may be others, but I wanted to at least share that with the Court in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you are aware of -- that such practice has been adopted in other Chambers in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I haven't personally encountered it, Your Honour, in the trials I've conducted. I'm certainly not disputing the Court's position that it has been done. On the other hand, to the extent that's the case, I'm not aware of the behind-the-scenes issues it may have given rise to and the -- the value-versus-cost equation involved. If -- I'd be happy to be directed to or I will certainly make every effort to inquire about cases in which that approach or a similar approach has been undertaken and see how successful it seems to have been and what problems, if any, it may have given rise to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But as Madam Uertz-Retzlaff indicated, if Prosecution is minded to produce only one statement per witness, there would be no problem on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's -- we understand the value of so doing. For one thing, it represents a -- the coherent -- in the cases of testimony, of coherent testimony by the witness in one relative sitting. So we do consider that ideal, but I'm also aware that there are circumstances where that's simply not possible. I do appreciate the fact that to the extent that that objective can be met, then it minimises the problem I may be raising. But I think it's fair to say that that won't be the case in every circumstance, and I'm not in a position at this moment to say precisely the percentage of cases in which it becomes an issue. I think we'll see -- even where we don't see one testimony supplanting all others, we're likely to see one testimony predominant and some significant but relatively small portions of other testimonies or statements also being elicited. So I think as a -- I understand the point made by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and the Court's reaction to it, but I don't think we can proffer it as a universal situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider your submission as well. I have three other matters in front of me --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have two questions in relation to 92 ter filings, and I would -- as it fits here I would like to raise it right now, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the associated exhibits, we had actually planned to prepare tables. Let's assume the situation we have picked one testimony and we would offer tables in which we list all these exhibits that are either tendered through that witness in their testimony or referred to by the witness. We would list them even though in cases where we would want to -- we do not intend to tender them through that witness. We would actually like in the 92 bis filings -- we would list all these exhibits, notice in a special column whether we want to tender these exhibits through this particular witness, but at the same time Dr. Karadzic would see which other exhibits the witness had referred to or had been put to him, for instance, Defence exhibits, and could then choose to address those. We thought that would be quite a fair process, and therefore this is what we actually intended to do, if you agreed to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, there is no reason not to admit it, but I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Karadzic, on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence needs to read everything that pertains to a particular witness. You are right. This means focusing and narrowing down the issues that we are going to deal with, and yes, that will be of assistance. But we still need to study and review everything that has ever been stated by a particular witness. The same applies to all other issues concerning the scope of the Prosecution case. If there is a single incident in a municipality, I need to deal with the entire municipality and the climate that existed there and the circumstances and so on. At any rate, what is the most important issue here for the Defence is when we will be disclosed the 92 ter package. Another issue that is important is that the summary must be disclosed publicly, in a public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, the practice you suggested is highly recommendable in the view of the Chamber. What is your second observation?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The second point is during the preparation of these tables - and we actually are already doing this since quite some time - we have realised that some of the exhibits being referred to or tendered in the previous testimony of the witness are not on the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list. The question is: Do you want them all to be added in a supplementary exhibit list, or should we simply leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, my reaction is that it may depend upon your intention, whether the Prosecution is minded to tender those documents as evidence or not. If yes, it should be added to the 65 ter list; otherwise, I see no reason it should be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to avoid any surprises. I would like to receive this evidence well in advance. If they are not on the list of 65 ter, I know nothing about them and my teams on the ground also have to deal with that. I'm not going to prepare any surprises for the other party, therefore they shouldn't do the same to me. Your Excellency, there are about 45.000 documents, and I still don't know which one of them is going to be presented or not. I'm still wasting my time going through the material, of which perhaps only one-fourth would be presented to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are two categories of exhibits referred to -- documents referred to in -- for example, in one of the 92 ter witness statements. One would be the documents the Prosecution is minded to tender as evidence, and the other is ones the Prosecution is not minded to tender as evidence, but they're going to disclose the list of those documents for your information. So although they will not be listed in their 65 ter list, they should be included in so -- as you put it, in 65 ter -- I'm sorry, 92 ter package. And then I take it that the Prosecution, bearing in mind your need, they will be -- exercise their functions in a timely manner. So that exhausted your questions. So I'll turn to the issue of 92 bis witnesses -- oh, there's one further thing: Order of witnesses and notice of it. The Chamber is minded to order the Prosecution -- parties, but the Prosecution in the first instance, to file bimonthly, monthly, and weekly lists of the witnesses it will bring in order of their intended appearance. Each monthly list will be due on the 15th of the preceding month. However, on our working assumption that the trial will commence on 21st of October, the Prosecution should file immediately the list of witnesses for the remainder of October as well as for November and December. And on 15th of October, it should file its more detailed list of witnesses for the month of November as well as October. This procedure will be set out in detail in the Chamber's written order. Let me deal with the 92 bis motions first. Now that the Chamber has rendered its Rule 73 bis decision, the Chamber will begin finalising and issuing its decisions on various motions filed by the Prosecution for the admission of witness evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. We note that you, Mr. Karadzic, filed an omnibus response to these motions on 8th of July, 2009, and that the former Pre-Trial Judge informed you that you could file further responses at any time up to the Chamber's determination of these motions. Indeed, you have filed a response to the fifth motion for admission of Rule 92 bis evidence insofar as it relates to one particular witness. The Chamber is conscious of your efforts to interview Prosecution witnesses and to agree, where possible, to the admission of their evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis following your interviews with them and the submission of initial evidence you consider important. However, it is now important for the Chamber's decision on these Rule 92 bis motions to be finalised so that the Prosecution is aware which of its witnesses it needs to bring to give oral testimony or for cross-examination. For this reason we cannot wait indefinitely for you to file further responses in relation to individual proposed Rule 92 bis witnesses. So I'm letting you know that these decisions will be issued in the coming few weeks. The Chamber will make its own assessment of whether the requirements of admission of evidence under Rule 92 bis are met. Should we admit the evidence of a witness under Rule 92 bis whose evidence you would wish to supplement with your own Rule 92 bis statement, you are free to file a motion to that effect. As I said at the beginning, the Chamber is still considering the various other matters raised in the parties' submission on the trial procedure, and we will issue our order very soon following this Pre-Trial Conference. Is there any other item falling under this heading that anyone wishes to raise today before we finalise that order? I give the floor to the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the 92 bis decisions that are upcoming, we would -- it would be very helpful for the Prosecution if you would start with looking at our submission in relation to the Sarajevo shelling and sniping incidents because that's the component of the case that will go first. So it would be very helpful to have a decision on this issue. In relation to this, there is an issue with the interviewing of witnesses that Dr. Karadzic has actually embarked to go so that he can make meaningful suggestions for the 92 bis filings. The problem is so far we have only had two interviews conducted, and we have three interviews scheduled but they were cancelled, and nothing else seems to be forthcoming. So I don't know how we could factor this in. I mean, it was a useful exercise and you have already seen result of this in relation to one witness, but we are not actually doing much Defence interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "We" being Dr. Karadzic and the Defence team having interview with the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So far two witnesses were interviewed, and one of them was a 92 bis witness and he has made submissions on how he agrees to admitting this evidence 92 bis and has actually made a supplementary filing to this effect. And -- but that's the only one so far, and I do not see that any other interviews of 92 bis witnesses are scheduled, and I don't really see it happening now that the trial starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Excellencies. You have seen for yourselves that this is an extremely useful exercise and probably the majority of these witnesses would have been accepted by our side under the terms and conditions under which these interviews were conducted. Sixty witnesses accepted to have contacts with the Defence. As far as 92 bis is concerned, Your Excellency said that not all the 1200 [as interpreted] witnesses would be accepted. It would be very useful for us to know which witnesses are going to remain within the remit of 92 bis and which witnesses will have to appear here in person. I would kindly ask for a possibility to interview them when they come here. I had one interview with a 92 ter witness, which was very beneficial. Once the Trial Chamber decides which witnesses are not going to be accepted under 92 bis and if OTP still persist in their intention to call these witnesses, I will therefore request respectfully to interview them, just like I did with this 92 ter, that is to say to conduct interviews with them once they arrive here and before they give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your submission is helpful, so much so that we can now understand that it is in the interest of you and justice for us to expedite the issuing -- issue the decision as soon as possible. Apart from 92 bis issue, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any issues to raise in relation to the trial procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Is there anything else on the agenda? No, as I suppose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have something else, but I will give you the floor to address the Court as to the issues which relate to the trial procedure or procedural guide-line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would like to express my gratitude to you and the Chamber for taking seriously into consideration the difficulties faced by the Defence with the voluminous material and the commencement of the trial, particularly with regard to the witnesses. The OTP witness -- 92 ter witnesses will be dealt with by the OTP for a very brief time. However, the Defence has to deal with much more material than stipulated by the 92 ter summary. As far as that is concerned, I hope that the Chamber will accept that the Defence should be granted much more time than the OTP and that all the abridgments announced by the OTP and with regard to the material that I have to deal with is not of much help to me. I still need ample time in order to review everything that concerns each particular witness and for me to be able to achieve -- to challenge certain things. Therefore, the Defence allocated to the time should not be correlated with the time used by the OTP, but rather with each particular witness on a case-by-case basis. If the Defence manages to be fully prepared for the period of time saved, that will curtail the duration of this trial and this is going to be beneficial during the proceedings itself. Now, that as far as the witnesses are concerned and the time issue, which, in my mind, is very important. Also crucial is transparency and the timing of disclosure, and in that respect you have given the right to Defence to have everything available in time and in an orderly manner. I must say that the law -- the majority of the material we received since mid-May until today, but we still miss certain material. Papers are rather submitted in a chaotic manner, and we are wasting too much time in trying to put them in order. The esteemed Registrar, I must say, is in a sort of a -- protecting this institution from my interviews in the media, but I hope that in this courtroom I will have an opportunity to challenge the credibility and the conduct of all participants in our crisis, particularly those who are accusing me and putting forward certain allegations. Therefore, those who are accusing me have to subject themselves to my scrutiny of their role and their integrity and possibly their interest to demonstrate that they are either biassed or not biassed. When I say "those who are accusing me," I'm not referring to the OTP; I'm referring to a number of major countries who call themselves the international community and who operate through the United Nations. Therefore, I should be given an opportunity to demonstrate how the UN and UNPROFOR had been abused in this war. How can I defend myself if I cannot raise the issue of the responsibility of other participants and the conduct that affected our conduct as well? We did not act in a vacuum. We were faced with challenges that were jeopardising our survival. So let us prepare ourselves for the possibility for me to ask questions concerning the role of certain United Nations member states and address -- respect -- I'm expecting certain documents to be provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I merely stood because it became apparent and I wanted to make -- well, to curtail an unnecessary advance proffer of alleged relevance to anticipated cross-examination questions. I don't think this is the time or place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a criminal proceedings, different from a fact-finding mission for the purpose of the history finding or anything else. So -- but as far as the time for cross-examination is concerned to which he referred briefly, the Trial Chamber will not at the present time set a specific time-limit on cross-examining party for the cross-examination of the opposing party's witness. However, that said, the cross-examination should be limited to relevant and material matters. So the cross-examining party should use its best efforts to avoid unnecessary, irrelevant, or repetitive questioning of the opposing party's witness as a general rule. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in relation to cross-examination, Dr. Karadzic has actually in paragraph 18 of his submissions on the procedures made a very concrete proposal that we actually would oppose. We would suggest another course of action in this regard. We would suggest that in his oral request for additional time when his cross-examination time comes to an end, Dr. Karadzic should not only list the general topics, but rather provide details of the evidence he expects to elicitate from the witness. That would actually give the Trial Chamber the information it would need to make a determination. I do not think that it makes any sense to later on prepare an offer of proof and file it with the Trial Chamber. Such a written offer of proof the Prosecution would definitely move to strike. So I would suggest that he would rather make these submissions orally before a decision is taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of dealing with that issue in vacuum, how about dealing with the issue when and if it arises, during the course of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be included in our order to be followed. This trial will be conducted under the e-court system -- give me a minute. So the general principle will be that the -- all documents shall be handled through this system. However, in terms of practicality, I was informed that the access to all the e-court material from your seat you are currently seated is not possible. So my understanding is that you have -- during the course of trial, you have to be seated -- so you have to sit in one row forward and with your legal associates being seated immediately in front of you. And there are a couple minor issues I would like to raise. First thing is related to Rule 70 witnesses. The Chamber has issued a decision concerning the Rule 70 conditions placed on the evidence of witnesses 240 and has received the motion from Mr. Karadzic for the recision or variation of very similar conditions placed on the evidence of witness number 314. Insofar as these conditions relate to the testimony to be given by these two witnesses and the manner in which it is to be given, the Chamber has to determine whether to allow these trial-related conditions to remain in place or to exclude the evidence of these two witnesses on the basis that it is -- its probative value is outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. So we are minded to do that very soon and would be assisted in this matter by hearing from the Prosecution on whether it still intends to call these two witnesses subject to the trial-related conditions in place. So should we wish to -- should you wish to go into private session in order to discuss this, we can do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there is a need for this as long as we just refer to these two witnesses as the two witnesses. We still intend to call them, and we had actually planned to file submissions -- a motion for a trial-related protective measures closer to the time they would be called. However, if you want us to do that earlier, we can do that earlier as soon as you like it. Because we -- from the wording in the decision that you referred to, we got the understanding that the Trial Chamber would prefer to receive that -- these submissions at a later date. But if you prefer to have them now, we can file them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Thank you. One final thing I would like to comment is the -- is regarding pending motions. There are a number of other motions pending before this Chamber in addition to those before Appeals Chamber and one before a three-Judge Panel. Of those to be dealt with by this Chamber, the large majority of motions submitted by the accused for binding orders or the production of documents by various states on motions for the admission of evidence in writing submitted by the Prosecution. The binding order motions are being actively considered by the Chamber and we have taken a number of necessary steps to move their resolution forwards. This procedure takes some time, but please be assured, Mr. Karadzic, that we are dealing with them as quickly as possible. I have already mentioned the Rule 92 bis decisions which will be rendered soon, and the same applies to the Chamber's decision on the second Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts, which should be issued before the end of this week. That leaves one last Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts which is pending a response from the accused. That said, I think I exhausted all the bullet points I prepared, so I'd like to know whether there are any other further matters for the parties to raise. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I would like to point out two or three matters. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that needs to be demonstrated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- I think it's okay for the moment. So we have your submission, so you don't have to repeat what you stated in your submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, the other side repeated it so I did the same thing, repetition follows repetition. As for the other matter, I'm grateful to the Chamber for their understanding; namely, this trial cannot be transparent unless it is prepared well, unless all of the arguments are in place. The countries that are asking for this Tribunal to be shut down, that are asking for the proceedings to be speeded up are not submitting documents in a timely manner. And without their cooperation, this trial can never be fair. Therefore, I expect that you will urge these countries to provide these documents as soon as possible. Further on into the trial we will have even more sensitive documents. These documents that we have requested so far are not as sensitive, and we have not encountered as many problems in receiving them until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see to it that -- I noted that you were on your feet, Mr. Tieger. Did you mean to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It just concerns the issue of a redaction which we're sending to the Registry at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you've heard that the procedure is going to be used where the e-court system is going to be central. Now, I understand that you've had some training in the e-court techniques. Do you feel that that's sufficient or you -- do you require further training?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I had a very brief training. They promised to provide a server for me that I would be able to use from my room. So far that hasn't happened and probably will not be put in place before the end of the year. I will probably have an associate helping me with this. I don't expect this to be a huge problem if I have enough time to prepare my Defence case and to prepare myself for this trial, and during that period of time I will also train myself in the use of e-court. The material that I have to use is huge, over 1 million pages, over 300 days of testimony, audio and video material, this is a huge amount and I will need every kind of assistance imaginable. First, I will need to have sufficient time for preparation and I will need training; and without that it would be even harder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then the hearing is adjourned until the commencement of the trial which will be notified in due course.
